title: RAG end to end in code
scopeHtml: Scope: Why RAG exists and the full pipeline (ingest, chunk, embed, store, retrieve, rerank, prompt, generate), citations and "I don't know", evaluation, caching and freshness, production failure modes, and Spring AI / LangChain4j / Python implementations.

notes.title: Why RAG exists
notes.html:
The problem. A large language model (LLM) is a program that predicts the next piece of text. It learned from a huge text snapshot (its training data) that stopped at a knowledge cutoff date. So it knows nothing about your company's refund policy, last week's release notes or your private wiki. If you ask anyway, it may produce a confident, fluent, wrong answer. That is called a hallucination.

Three ways to give a model new knowledge.

Approach What it means Good for Weak at
Paste everything in the prompt Put all documents in the context window (the maximum text, measured in tokens, a model can read at once) Tiny corpora Cost, latency, limits, "lost in the middle"
Fine-tuning Train the model further on your data Style, format, behaviour Fresh facts, citations, deleting data
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) Search your documents at question time, paste only the relevant pieces, then ask the model Private, large or changing knowledge Needs a good search step

RAG in one sentence. Before asking the model, you retrieve the few passages most relevant to the question and augment the prompt with them, so the model generates an answer from evidence instead of memory.

Why companies choose it.

  • Notion AI Q&A, Glean, Microsoft Copilot over SharePoint and Intercom Fin all answer from the customer's own documents, with source links.
  • Knowledge changes by updating a document or index entry, not by retraining.
  • Access control can be applied per document at retrieval time (a user only gets passages they may see).
  • Answers can show sources, which builds trust and makes errors debuggable.

Real-life analogy. An open-book exam. The student (the model) is clever but has not memorised your textbook. RAG is the librarian who hands over the right three pages before the student writes the answer.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "RAG replaces fine-tuning". They solve different problems: RAG gives facts, fine-tuning shapes behaviour.
  • Saying "long context makes RAG obsolete". Large windows cost money and latency per call, and quality still drops with noise; retrieval stays cheaper and enables access control and citations.
  • Claiming RAG removes hallucination. It reduces it; the model can still ignore or misread the passages.

notes.title: The pipeline end to end
notes.html:
RAG has two separate phases. Ingestion runs ahead of time (or on a schedule). Query time runs on every user question.

INGESTION (offline)
 documents --> parse --> chunk --> embed --> vector store (+ metadata)

QUERY (online)
 question --> embed --> vector search (top-K) --> [rerank] --> build prompt
          --> LLM generate --> answer + citations

Terms you need.

  • Chunk: a small piece of a document (for example 200 to 500 words), the unit you search over.
  • Embedding: a list of numbers (a vector, typically hundreds to a few thousand numbers) produced by an embedding model so that texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions.
  • Vector store: a database that stores vectors and quickly returns the nearest ones to a query vector (FAISS, pgvector, Qdrant, Pinecone, and so on).
  • Top-K: the K best-scoring chunks returned by the search.
  • Reranker: a second, slower but more accurate model that re-orders the top-K by relevance to the question.
  • Grounding: forcing the answer to rest on the supplied passages.

Why two phases. Embedding a million chunks is slow and costly, so you do it once. A user question needs only one small embedding plus a fast nearest-neighbour search, so query time stays under about a second before the LLM call.

Real products. Perplexity is "search plus LLM". GitHub Copilot Chat retrieves code snippets from your repo before answering. Customer-support bots retrieve help-centre articles.

Real-life analogy. A restaurant: ingestion is the kitchen prepping and labelling ingredients in the morning; query time is the cook grabbing exactly the labelled jars needed for one order.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up the embedding model used at ingest and query time. They must be the same model, or the vectors live in different spaces.
  • Forgetting that RAG quality is capped by retrieval: if the right chunk is not in top-K, the best LLM cannot recover it.
  • Treating the LLM as the only component to tune. Most failures are in chunking and retrieval.

notes.title: Ingest and chunk
notes.html:
What ingestion does. Load raw files (PDF, HTML, Markdown, Confluence pages, Jira tickets), extract clean text, split it into chunks, and attach metadata (source, title, page, section, author, date, access group).

Why chunk at all. An embedding of a whole 50-page PDF blurs every topic into one vector, and you cannot paste 50 pages for every question. A chunk should hold roughly one idea.

Common chunking strategies.

  • Fixed size with overlap: for example 500 tokens with 50 to 100 tokens of overlap, so a sentence cut at the boundary still appears whole in a neighbour. Simple and a fine default.
  • Structure-aware: split on headings, paragraphs, Markdown sections, code functions. Better quality for docs and code.
  • Semantic: split where the topic changes (compare neighbouring sentence embeddings). More expensive.
  • Parent-child: search small chunks for precision, but send the larger parent section to the LLM for context.

Always keep the heading path ("Billing > Refunds") inside or beside the chunk; a chunk saying "within 30 days" is meaningless without knowing it is about refunds.

doc.md --> split by heading --> 500-token windows (overlap 50)
        --> {text, source="refund-policy.md", section="Refunds", page=3}

A minimal splitter in all three languages (words stand in for tokens to stay simple; real systems count tokens):

def chunk(text: str, size: int = 200, overlap: int = 40) -> list[str]:
    words = text.split()
    step = size - overlap
    return [" ".join(words[i:i + size]) for i in range(0, max(len(words) - overlap, 1), step)]

print(len(chunk("word " * 1000)))  # prints 7: 1000 words, windows of 200 stepping by 160
fun chunk(text: String, size: Int = 200, overlap: Int = 40): List<String> {
    val words = text.split(Regex("\\s+")).filter { it.isNotEmpty() }
    val step = size - overlap
    return (0 until maxOf(words.size - overlap, 1) step step)
        .map { words.subList(it, minOf(it + size, words.size)).joinToString(" ") }
}

fun main() = println(chunk("word ".repeat(1000)).size) // prints 7
import java.util.*;

public class Chunker {
    static List<String> chunk(String text, int size, int overlap) {
        String[] w = text.trim().split("\\s+");
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        int step = size - overlap;
        for (int i = 0; i < Math.max(w.length - overlap, 1); i += step) {
            out.add(String.join(" ", Arrays.copyOfRange(w, i, Math.min(i + size, w.length))));
        }
        return out;
    }

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(chunk("word ".repeat(1000), 200, 40).size()); // prints 7
    }
}

Real-world notes.

  • Unstructured, LlamaParse, Apache Tika and Azure Document Intelligence are common parsers. PDFs with tables and scans (needing OCR) are the number one source of garbage text.
  • Strip headers, footers and navigation menus; repeated boilerplate pollutes search results.
  • Store a stable document ID and a content hash so you can update or delete exactly the right chunks later.

Real-life analogy. Cutting a textbook into index cards. Too big and a card covers ten topics; too small and a card says "yes, see above". Writing the chapter name at the top of each card is the metadata.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing chunk size by gut feeling. It must be tuned with a retrieval evaluation (see the evaluation section).
  • Splitting mid-table or mid-code-block, which destroys meaning.
  • Dropping metadata, which blocks filtering, citations and per-user access control later.

notes.title: Embed and store
notes.html:
Embedding recap. An embedding model turns text into a vector. Similar meaning means a small angle between vectors. The usual score is cosine similarity: 1 means same direction, 0 unrelated.

Which model. Anthropic does not offer its own embedding model; its docs point to providers such as Voyage AI (verify in the docs). Other common choices: OpenAI text-embedding-3-*, Google Gemini embeddings, Cohere, or open models run locally (for example all-MiniLM-L6-v2 through sentence-transformers or LangChain4j's bundled ONNX version). The vector size (dimension) is fixed by the model; the store must be created with the same dimension.

Storing. Each row holds: vector, chunk text, metadata, document ID. Options:

  • FAISS: a library, in-process, great for prototypes and offline jobs.
  • pgvector: a PostgreSQL extension; use your existing database, SQL filters and transactions.
  • Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Pinecone: dedicated vector databases with filtering and scaling.

Nearest-neighbour search over millions of vectors uses ANN (approximate nearest neighbour) indexes such as HNSW, trading a little recall for large speed gains.

Below is a complete tiny in-memory "store" with a stand-in embed function. Replace embed with a real provider call; the rest is real.

import numpy as np

def embed(texts: list[str]) -> np.ndarray:
    # Replace with a real call, e.g. voyageai Client().embed(texts, model=..., input_type="document")
    # (verify in the provider docs). Returns shape (len(texts), dim), rows L2-normalised.
    raise NotImplementedError

class Store:
    def __init__(self):
        self.vecs, self.items = [], []

    def add(self, chunks: list[str], source: str):
        v = embed(chunks)
        self.vecs.extend(v)
        self.items.extend({"text": c, "source": source} for c in chunks)

    def search(self, qvec, k=4):
        scores = np.array(self.vecs) @ qvec          # cosine, since vectors are normalised
        top = np.argsort(-scores)[:k]
        return [(float(scores[i]), self.items[i]) for i in top]
// Plain-Kotlin store; embed() is a stand-in for a real embedding call.
data class Item(val text: String, val source: String)

fun embed(texts: List<String>): List<FloatArray> = TODO("call embedding provider; L2-normalise")

fun dot(a: FloatArray, b: FloatArray) = a.indices.sumOf { (a[it] * b[it]).toDouble() }

class Store {
    private val vecs = mutableListOf<FloatArray>()
    private val items = mutableListOf<Item>()

    fun add(chunks: List<String>, source: String) {
        vecs += embed(chunks)
        items += chunks.map { Item(it, source) }
    }

    fun search(q: FloatArray, k: Int = 4): List<Pair<Double, Item>> =
        vecs.indices.map { dot(vecs[it], q) to items[it] }
            .sortedByDescending { it.first }.take(k)
}
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class Store {
    record Item(String text, String source) {}
    record Hit(double score, Item item) {}

    final List<float[]> vecs = new ArrayList<>();
    final List<Item> items = new ArrayList<>();

    // Stand-in: call your embedding provider here and L2-normalise.
    static List<float[]> embed(List<String> texts) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }

    static double dot(float[] a, float[] b) {
        double s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) s += a[i] * b[i]; return s;
    }

    void add(List<String> chunks, String source) {
        vecs.addAll(embed(chunks));
        chunks.forEach(c -> items.add(new Item(c, source)));
    }

    List<Hit> search(float[] q, int k) {
        return IntStream.range(0, vecs.size())
            .mapToObj(i -> new Hit(dot(vecs.get(i), q), items.get(i)))
            .sorted(Comparator.comparingDouble(Hit::score).reversed())
            .limit(k).collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
}

Production details.

  • Embed in batches (dozens to hundreds of chunks per request) and respect rate limits with retries.
  • Record the embedding model name and version with each vector. Changing models means re-embedding everything.
  • Use upserts keyed by chunk ID so re-running ingestion is idempotent (safe to repeat).

Real-life analogy. A library where every book is shelved by "what it is about" rather than alphabetically, so a request for "how to get my money back" lands near the shelf labelled "refunds" even though the words differ.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing embedding models or dimensions between ingest and query (wrong or crashing results).
  • Not normalising vectors when the store assumes dot product equals cosine.
  • Forgetting some embedding APIs distinguish document and query input types (verify per provider).

notes.title: Retrieve and rerank
notes.html:
Retrieval. Embed the user question with the same model, ask the store for the top-K nearest chunks (K often 20 to 50 when a reranker follows, 3 to 8 when it does not).

Metadata filters. Combine vector search with filters: tenant_id = 42, lang = "en", updated_after = ..., user_groups IN (...). Filtering before or during search is how multi-tenant and permission-aware RAG stays safe. Never retrieve everything and filter in the UI.

Hybrid search. Embeddings capture meaning but can miss exact tokens such as error code E1042 or a product SKU. BM25 is classic keyword scoring. Hybrid search runs both and merges them, often with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (score = sum of 1/(60 + rank) across lists). Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Weaviate, Qdrant and pgvector with Postgres full-text all support it.

Reranking. The first search is fast but rough because query and chunk are embedded separately (a bi-encoder). A cross-encoder reranker reads question and chunk together and scores relevance more accurately, but is too slow for millions of chunks. So: retrieve 30 cheaply, rerank to the best 5. Cohere Rerank, Voyage rerank, bge-reranker and FlashRank are common choices.

question --> embed --> top 30 (vector + BM25, fused)
         --> cross-encoder rerank --> top 5 --> prompt

Reciprocal Rank Fusion is small enough to show in full (it merges two ranked lists of chunk IDs):

def rrf(*rankings: list[str], k: int = 60) -> list[str]:
    score: dict[str, float] = {}
    for ranking in rankings:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranking):
            score[doc_id] = score.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank + 1)
    return sorted(score, key=score.get, reverse=True)

print(rrf(["a", "b", "c"], ["b", "d", "a"]))  # prints ['b', 'a', 'd', 'c']
fun rrf(vararg rankings: List<String>, k: Int = 60): List<String> {
    val score = mutableMapOf<String, Double>()
    for (r in rankings) r.forEachIndexed { rank, id ->
        score[id] = (score[id] ?: 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank + 1)
    }
    return score.entries.sortedByDescending { it.value }.map { it.key }
}

fun main() = println(rrf(listOf("a", "b", "c"), listOf("b", "d", "a"))) // [b, a, d, c]
import java.util.*;

public class Rrf {
    static List<String> rrf(int k, List<List<String>> rankings) {
        Map<String, Double> score = new HashMap<>();
        for (List<String> r : rankings)
            for (int rank = 0; rank < r.size(); rank++)
                score.merge(r.get(rank), 1.0 / (k + rank + 1), Double::sum);
        List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(score.keySet());
        ids.sort((x, y) -> Double.compare(score.get(y), score.get(x)));
        return ids;
    }

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(rrf(60, List.of(List.of("a","b","c"), List.of("b","d","a")))); // [b, a, d, c]
    }
}

Other retrieval boosters. Query rewriting (the LLM turns "what about for Pro users?" into a standalone question using chat history), multi-query (several paraphrases, merge results), HyDE (embed a hypothetical answer instead of the question), MMR (maximal marginal relevance, avoids five near-duplicate chunks).

Real-life analogy. Hiring: a recruiter skims 500 CVs in a minute (vector search), then a hiring manager interviews the best 5 carefully (reranker).

Common interview traps.

  • Using only vector search for IDs, names and codes; keyword or hybrid search fixes this.
  • Skipping filters on tenant or permissions, which leaks data across customers.
  • Setting K too large; more chunks means more cost, more noise and an answer that drifts.

notes.title: Build the prompt and generate the answer
notes.html:
The idea. Put the retrieved chunks into the prompt in a clear structure, add firm instructions, then call the model. A system prompt is the standing instruction to the model; the user message carries the question and the context.

A good RAG prompt.

  • Say the model must answer only from the provided context.
  • Say what to do when the context is insufficient (see the next section).
  • Wrap each chunk with an ID and source, so the model can cite.
  • Separate untrusted document text from your instructions with tags (for example <doc id="1">...</doc>), because documents can contain prompt injection (hidden text such as "ignore previous instructions").
  • Use a low temperature (for example 0 to 0.2) for factual answers.
[system]  Answer ONLY from <documents>. Cite as [id]. If not found, say "I don't know".
[user]    <documents>
            <doc id="1" source="refund-policy.md">Refunds within 30 days...</doc>
            <doc id="2" source="faq.md">Digital goods are non-refundable...</doc>
          </documents>
          Question: Can I get a refund after 45 days?

End-to-end generation with Anthropic SDKs (API key read from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; model id claude-sonnet-5-5, verify current ids in the docs):

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

SYSTEM = ("Answer ONLY from the documents. Cite sources like [1]. "
          "If the documents do not contain the answer, reply exactly: I don't know.")

def answer(question: str, hits: list[dict]) -> str:
    docs = "\n".join(f'<doc id="{i+1}" source="{h["source"]}">{h["text"]}</doc>'
                     for i, h in enumerate(hits))
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=500, temperature=0, system=SYSTEM,
        messages=[{"role": "user",
                   "content": f"<documents>\n{docs}\n</documents>\n\nQuestion: {question}"}])
    return msg.content[0].text   # e.g. "No, refunds end after 30 days [1]."
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams

val client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv() // reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (verify in SDK docs)

const val SYSTEM = "Answer ONLY from the documents. Cite sources like [1]. " +
    "If the documents do not contain the answer, reply exactly: I don't know."

fun answer(question: String, hits: List<Pair<String, String>>): String { // (source, text)
    val docs = hits.mapIndexed { i, (src, text) -> """<doc id="${i + 1}" source="$src">$text</doc>""" }
        .joinToString("\n")
    val params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
        .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(500).temperature(0.0).system(SYSTEM)
        .addUserMessage("<documents>\n$docs\n</documents>\n\nQuestion: $question")
        .build()
    val msg = client.messages().create(params)
    return msg.content().first().text().get().text() // e.g. "No, refunds end after 30 days [1]."
}
import com.anthropic.client.AnthropicClient;
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient;
import com.anthropic.models.messages.Message;
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams;
import java.util.List;

public class RagAnswer {
    static final AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv(); // ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
    static final String SYSTEM = "Answer ONLY from the documents. Cite sources like [1]. "
        + "If the documents do not contain the answer, reply exactly: I don't know.";

    record Hit(String source, String text) {}

    static String answer(String question, List<Hit> hits) {
        StringBuilder docs = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < hits.size(); i++)
            docs.append("<doc id=\"%d\" source=\"%s\">%s</doc>\n"
                .formatted(i + 1, hits.get(i).source(), hits.get(i).text()));
        MessageCreateParams params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
            .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(500).temperature(0.0).system(SYSTEM)
            .addUserMessage("<documents>\n" + docs + "</documents>\n\nQuestion: " + question)
            .build();
        Message msg = client.messages().create(params);
        return msg.content().get(0).text().get().text(); // e.g. "No, refunds end after 30 days [1]."
    }
}

Token budget. Count: system prompt + question + K chunks + expected answer must fit in the context window. Cost grows linearly with the number of context tokens, and so does latency to the first token. Some models allow prompt caching for a repeated stable prefix (such as a big fixed instruction block); verify the current rules in the docs.

Real-life analogy. Handing a lawyer a folder with numbered exhibits and the instruction "argue only from these exhibits and cite the exhibit number".

Common interview traps.

  • Putting instructions and untrusted document text in one blob with no separation (injection risk).
  • Forgetting the answer budget (max_tokens) so replies are cut off mid-sentence.
  • Ignoring parameter limits: some newer models restrict sampling parameters such as temperature; check the docs for your model.

notes.title: Citations, grounding and "I don't know"
notes.html:
Grounding means every claim in the answer is supported by a retrieved passage. Citations make that visible: the answer carries markers like [1] that map to a source title, URL and page.

How to produce citations.

  1. Prompt-based: give chunks IDs, ask the model to cite IDs, then your code maps IDs back to sources. Works with any model. Validate that cited IDs exist; models sometimes invent a [7].
  2. Native citation features: some providers have a built-in citations option where you pass documents and the response returns spans pointing at the source text (Anthropic offers a citations feature; verify the current request format in the docs).
  3. Quote-then-answer: ask the model to first extract short verbatim quotes, then answer from them. Quotes can be checked with a simple string match.

"I don't know" behaviour. A good RAG system declines when evidence is missing. Layers of defence:

  • Prompt rule: "if not in documents, say you do not know".
  • Score threshold: if the best similarity is below a tuned cutoff, skip generation and return "no relevant document found" (or hand over to a human). This also saves an LLM call.
  • A post-check: ask a cheap model "is every claim supported by these passages? yes/no" (an LLM judge).

The validation step can be done in plain code, in all three languages:

import re

def check_citations(answer: str, n_docs: int) -> bool:
    ids = {int(m) for m in re.findall(r"\[(\d+)\]", answer)}
    return bool(ids) and all(1 <= i <= n_docs for i in ids)

print(check_citations("Refunds end after 30 days [1].", 2))  # True
print(check_citations("Yes you can [7].", 2))                # False (hallucinated id)
fun checkCitations(answer: String, nDocs: Int): Boolean {
    val ids = Regex("\\[(\\d+)]").findAll(answer).map { it.groupValues[1].toInt() }.toSet()
    return ids.isNotEmpty() && ids.all { it in 1..nDocs }
}

fun main() {
    println(checkCitations("Refunds end after 30 days [1].", 2)) // true
    println(checkCitations("Yes you can [7].", 2))               // false
}
import java.util.*;
import java.util.regex.*;

public class Cite {
    static boolean check(String answer, int nDocs) {
        Matcher m = Pattern.compile("\\[(\\d+)]").matcher(answer);
        Set<Integer> ids = new HashSet<>();
        while (m.find()) ids.add(Integer.parseInt(m.group(1)));
        return !ids.isEmpty() && ids.stream().allMatch(i -> i >= 1 && i <= nDocs);
    }

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(check("Refunds end after 30 days [1].", 2)); // true
        System.out.println(check("Yes you can [7].", 2));               // false
    }
}

Real products. Perplexity shows numbered sources beside every sentence. Enterprise search tools (Glean, Microsoft Copilot) link to the exact document and respect the asker's permissions. Medical and legal assistants often refuse rather than guess.

Real-life analogy. A student writing an essay with footnotes. A teacher can check each footnote; an essay without footnotes must be trusted blindly.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a citation proves correctness. The model can cite a real passage that does not support its claim, so verify entailment, not just existence.
  • One global similarity threshold copied from a blog. It depends on the embedding model and corpus; tune it on your own data.
  • Letting the model answer from general knowledge when retrieval returned nothing, which defeats the point of grounding.

notes.title: Evaluating retrieval and answers
notes.html:
Rule. Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. If you only look at final answers you cannot tell whether search or the model is at fault.

Build a golden set. 50 to 200 real questions, each with the expected source chunk(s) and a reference answer. Sources: support tickets, search logs, subject-matter experts, or LLM-generated questions reviewed by a human. Version it like code.

Retrieval metrics.

  • Recall@K (hit rate): fraction of questions whose correct chunk appears in the top K. The most important number.
  • MRR (mean reciprocal rank): average of 1/rank of the first correct chunk.
  • Precision@K and nDCG: how clean and well ordered the top K is.

Generation metrics.

  • Faithfulness / groundedness: are all claims supported by the retrieved context?
  • Answer relevance: does it answer the question asked?
  • Correctness against the reference answer.
  • Usually scored by an LLM judge with a rubric, spot-checked by humans. Frameworks: Ragas, TruLens, DeepEval, promptfoo (verify current features).
def recall_at_k(results: dict[str, list[str]], gold: dict[str, str], k: int = 5) -> float:
    hits = sum(gold[q] in results[q][:k] for q in gold)
    return hits / len(gold)

print(recall_at_k({"q1": ["c9", "c2"], "q2": ["c5", "c1"]}, {"q1": "c2", "q2": "c7"}))  # 0.5
fun recallAtK(results: Map<String, List<String>>, gold: Map<String, String>, k: Int = 5): Double =
    gold.count { (q, id) -> id in results.getValue(q).take(k) }.toDouble() / gold.size

fun main() = println(
    recallAtK(mapOf("q1" to listOf("c9", "c2"), "q2" to listOf("c5", "c1")),
              mapOf("q1" to "c2", "q2" to "c7"))) // 0.5
import java.util.*;

public class Eval {
    static double recallAtK(Map<String, List<String>> results, Map<String, String> gold, int k) {
        long hits = gold.entrySet().stream().filter(e -> {
            List<String> r = results.get(e.getKey());
            return r.subList(0, Math.min(k, r.size())).contains(e.getValue());
        }).count();
        return (double) hits / gold.size();
    }

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(recallAtK(
            Map.of("q1", List.of("c9", "c2"), "q2", List.of("c5", "c1")),
            Map.of("q1", "c2", "q2", "c7"), 5)); // 0.5
    }
}

In practice. Run the golden set in CI whenever you change chunk size, embedding model, prompt or K; fail the build if recall or faithfulness drops. In production, log question, retrieved IDs, answer and user feedback (thumbs up/down), then add bad cases to the golden set.

Real-life analogy. A driving test with two parts: can you find the right route (retrieval), and do you drive it safely (generation). Failing the exam does not tell you which part failed unless you score them separately.

Common interview traps.

  • Evaluating by "it looked good on five demo questions".
  • Using an LLM judge from the same model family with no human calibration; judges have biases (prefer long answers, prefer their own style).
  • Measuring only answer quality and then tuning the prompt when the real fault is recall.

notes.title: Caching and keeping data fresh
notes.html:
Cost and latency map. A RAG request has up to four costs: embedding the question, vector search, reranking and the LLM call. The LLM call is usually the largest in both money and time.

What to cache.

  • Embedding cache: key = hash of text and model; avoids re-embedding repeated questions and unchanged chunks at ingest.
  • Retrieval cache: normalised question to top-K IDs, short TTL (time-to-live).
  • Response cache: exact question plus same context to saved answer. Safe for identical inputs only.
  • Semantic cache: if a new question's embedding is very close to a past one, reuse the past answer. Big savings on FAQs, but a wrong threshold returns wrong answers ("cancel order" vs "cancel subscription"), and it must be keyed by tenant and permissions.
  • Prompt caching (provider feature): reuse the processed prefix of a long stable prompt at lower cost; verify exact rules and minimum sizes in the provider docs.

A small exact-match cache with TTL in all three languages:

import time, hashlib

_cache: dict[str, tuple[float, str]] = {}

def cached(question: str, ttl: float, compute) -> str:
    key = hashlib.sha256(question.strip().lower().encode()).hexdigest()
    hit = _cache.get(key)
    if hit and time.time() - hit[0] < ttl:
        return hit[1]                      # cache hit: no LLM call
    value = compute(question)
    _cache[key] = (time.time(), value)
    return value
import java.security.MessageDigest

private val cache = HashMap<String, Pair<Long, String>>()

fun cached(question: String, ttlMs: Long, compute: (String) -> String): String {
    val key = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
        .digest(question.trim().lowercase().toByteArray()).joinToString("") { "%02x".format(it) }
    cache[key]?.let { (t, v) -> if (System.currentTimeMillis() - t < ttlMs) return v } // hit
    return compute(question).also { cache[key] = System.currentTimeMillis() to it }
}
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.Function;

public class Cache {
    record Entry(long at, String value) {}
    static final Map<String, Entry> cache = new HashMap<>();

    static String cached(String q, long ttlMs, Function<String, String> compute) throws Exception {
        byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(q.trim().toLowerCase().getBytes());
        String key = HexFormat.of().formatHex(d);
        Entry e = cache.get(key);
        if (e != null && System.currentTimeMillis() - e.at() < ttlMs) return e.value(); // hit
        String v = compute.apply(q);
        cache.put(key, new Entry(System.currentTimeMillis(), v));
        return v;
    }
}

(Real services use Redis or Caffeine instead of a map, with eviction and size limits.)

Freshness. Documents change; stale chunks give stale answers.

  • Incremental ingestion: store a content hash per document. On each run, re-chunk and re-embed only changed documents, upsert new chunks and delete chunks of removed documents or the old version's leftover chunks.
  • Triggers: webhooks (Confluence, Google Drive, GitHub), a scheduled crawl (nightly), or a change-data-capture stream from the source database.
  • Metadata for time: store updated_at and prefer newer documents, or filter by date for "latest" questions.
  • Deletion and compliance: when a user or document must be forgotten, delete the vectors too; this is a real advantage over fine-tuning.
  • Re-embedding migrations: when switching embedding models, build a second index, backfill, switch traffic, then delete the old one.

Real-life analogy. A newspaper stand: caching is keeping yesterday's most-asked-for paper under the counter; freshness is replacing it when today's edition arrives, and pulling any copy that was recalled.

Common interview traps.

  • A semantic cache shared across users or tenants, leaking one person's answer to another.
  • Forgetting to delete old chunks when a document shrinks, leaving ghost passages in search results.
  • Re-embedding the entire corpus on every run instead of hashing for changes.

notes.title: Failure modes and debugging in production
notes.html:
When a RAG answer is wrong, walk the pipeline in order. The first broken stage is the culprit.

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Answer ignores the fact you know exists Chunk never retrieved (bad chunking, missing in index, wrong embedding) Check recall; fix chunking, add hybrid search, re-ingest
Right chunk retrieved but answer wrong Chunk buried among noise or model misread Rerank, lower K, restructure prompt, stronger model
Confident answer with no source support Model used its own memory Stricter prompt, threshold, groundedness check
Contradicting answers Old and new document versions both indexed Versioning, delete stale chunks, date filters
Answer cut in the middle Context too long or max_tokens too small Trim chunks, raise limit
"Lost in the middle" Important chunk in the middle of a long context Fewer chunks, put the best at start or end
Wrong answers on tables or numbers Bad PDF parsing Better parser, keep tables as Markdown
Another customer's data appears Missing tenant filter Enforce filters in the store query, test it
Odd instructions obeyed Prompt injection inside a document Delimit documents, sanitise, limit tool powers, review
High latency Too many chunks, slow reranker, no streaming Smaller K, cache, stream the answer
Bills growing Large contexts, no caching Cap K and tokens, cache, route easy questions to smaller models

Observability. Log per request: question, rewritten query, retrieved chunk IDs with scores, final prompt size in tokens, model, latency per stage, answer, user feedback. Tools: Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, OpenTelemetry traces (verify current products). Without these logs you cannot debug a bad answer after the fact.

Real incident pattern. A support bot starts quoting a discontinued price. Investigation: the new pricing page was ingested, but the old page's chunks were never deleted, and both scored highly. Fix: delete by document ID on update, add updated_at preference, add a regression question to the golden set.

Real-life analogy. A plumber tracing a leak: start at the tap and follow the pipe upstream until you find the first wet spot, rather than replacing the tap.

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to "use a bigger model" before checking whether retrieval found the right chunk.
  • Having no logs of retrieved chunks, so failures cannot be reproduced.
  • Believing a single fix (like a bigger K) helps everywhere; it often trades recall for noise.

notes.title: Implementing with Spring AI, LangChain4j and Python frameworks
notes.html:
You rarely hand-roll everything. Frameworks supply loaders, splitters, vector store adapters and chains. Versions and package names move fast; treat the snippets as shapes and verify against the current docs.

Spring AI (Java/Kotlin backends). Provides VectorStore (adapters for pgvector, Qdrant, Redis, Chroma and others), EmbeddingModel, ChatClient, document readers/transformers (including TokenTextSplitter) and an advisor, QuestionAnswerAdvisor, that does retrieve-then-augment for you.

LangChain4j (Java/Kotlin). Provides EmbeddingModel, EmbeddingStore, ContentRetriever, DocumentSplitters, and AI Services (an interface that LangChain4j implements, wiring the retriever into the chat model).

Python. Either raw SDK calls plus FAISS/pgvector/Qdrant client (most transparent, ideal for learning and for small production services), or LangChain / LlamaIndex when you want ready-made loaders, rerankers and evaluators.

The same job in each ecosystem. First, Python with FAISS (the vectors come from an embed function like the one above):

import faiss, numpy as np

# vecs: float32 array (n, dim), rows L2-normalised, from embed(chunks)
def build_index(vecs: np.ndarray) -> faiss.IndexFlatIP:
    index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(vecs.shape[1])   # inner product == cosine on normalised vectors
    index.add(vecs.astype("float32"))
    return index

def retrieve(index, chunks, qvec, k=4):
    scores, ids = index.search(qvec.astype("float32").reshape(1, -1), k)
    return [(float(s), chunks[i]) for s, i in zip(scores[0], ids[0]) if i != -1]

Kotlin with Spring AI (a service where VectorStore and ChatClient.Builder are auto-configured by Spring Boot starters):

import org.springframework.ai.chat.client.ChatClient
import org.springframework.ai.chat.client.advisor.QuestionAnswerAdvisor
import org.springframework.ai.document.Document
import org.springframework.ai.vectorstore.VectorStore
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service

@Service
class RagService(private val store: VectorStore, builder: ChatClient.Builder) {
    // Advisor class/package names changed across Spring AI versions: verify in the reference docs.
    private val chat = builder.defaultAdvisors(QuestionAnswerAdvisor.builder(store).build()).build()

    fun ingest(texts: List<String>, source: String) =
        store.add(texts.map { Document(it, mapOf("source" to source)) }) // embeds + stores

    fun ask(question: String): String? =
        chat.prompt().user(question).call().content() // retrieves top chunks, augments, generates
}

Java with LangChain4j (in-memory store and a bundled local embedding model; swap in pgvector or Qdrant for production):

import dev.langchain4j.data.document.Document;
import dev.langchain4j.data.document.splitter.DocumentSplitters;
import dev.langchain4j.data.embedding.Embedding;
import dev.langchain4j.data.segment.TextSegment;
import dev.langchain4j.model.embedding.EmbeddingModel;
import dev.langchain4j.model.embedding.onnx.allminilml6v2.AllMiniLmL6V2EmbeddingModel;
import dev.langchain4j.store.embedding.EmbeddingSearchRequest;
import dev.langchain4j.store.embedding.EmbeddingStore;
import dev.langchain4j.store.embedding.inmemory.InMemoryEmbeddingStore;

public class LcRag {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EmbeddingModel model = new AllMiniLmL6V2EmbeddingModel();
        EmbeddingStore<TextSegment> store = new InMemoryEmbeddingStore<>();

        var splitter = DocumentSplitters.recursive(500, 50);          // size, overlap (characters)
        for (TextSegment seg : splitter.split(Document.from("Refunds are allowed within 30 days."))) {
            store.add(model.embed(seg).content(), seg);
        }

        Embedding q = model.embed("Can I get my money back?").content();
        var result = store.search(EmbeddingSearchRequest.builder()
            .queryEmbedding(q).maxResults(3).minScore(0.5).build()); // verify builder in current docs
        result.matches().forEach(m -> System.out.println(m.score() + " " + m.embedded().text()));
        // prints a score near 0.6-0.8 and the refund sentence
    }
}

The Python and Kotlin versions use the same shape in each ecosystem: ingest, embed, store, retrieve, augment, generate. Kotlin can also call LangChain4j directly (it is a JVM library) in the same way as the Java snippet.

Which to pick.

  • Spring Boot shop with Postgres: Spring AI or LangChain4j with pgvector; one database, familiar transactions.
  • Android: do not embed or call the LLM from the app with a key. The app calls your backend, which runs the RAG pipeline (on-device RAG is possible for small private corpora but is a separate topic).
  • Data-science team iterating quickly: Python with LlamaIndex or LangChain, then port hot paths.

Real-life analogy. Assembling flat-pack furniture versus carving it from a log. Frameworks give you the parts and a manual; you still need to know what a good chair looks like.

Common interview traps.

  • Copying framework snippets without knowing the defaults (chunk size, K, similarity threshold, prompt template). Defaults are rarely right for your data.
  • Mixing versions: Spring AI and LangChain4j have changed class names between releases; pin versions.
  • Hiding the pipeline behind a one-line chain and then being unable to log or evaluate each stage.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• RAG = retrieve relevant chunks, put them in the prompt, generate a grounded answer. It supplies private, fresh knowledge without retraining and enables citations and access control.
  • Ingestion (parse, chunk, embed, store with metadata) is offline; query time (embed question, search, rerank, prompt, generate) is online. Use the same embedding model for both.
  • Chunk by structure with overlap and metadata; tune size by measuring recall, not guessing.
  • Retrieve more than you need (top 20 to 50), use hybrid vector plus BM25 search with filters, rerank to a few (3 to 8), and always enforce tenant and permission filters inside the query.
  • Prompt: system rules to answer only from delimited documents, numbered sources, low temperature, an explicit "I don't know" path, plus a similarity threshold and citation validation.
  • Evaluate retrieval (Recall@K, MRR) and generation (faithfulness, relevance) separately on a golden set, and run it in CI.
  • Cache embeddings, retrievals and answers carefully (never across tenants); keep data fresh with content hashes, upserts and deletes.
  • Debug stage by stage: was the chunk indexed, retrieved, ranked, used? Log retrieved IDs and scores for every request.
  • Spring AI, LangChain4j, LangChain/LlamaIndex or raw SDK + FAISS/pgvector all implement the same pipeline; know the defaults and pin versions.

questions.promptHtml: What is RAG, and what problem does it solve that a plain LLM call does not?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks you understand the problem before the tooling. Many candidates can name the acronym but cannot say why the model needs help.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An LLM (large language model, a program that predicts the next piece of text) only knows what was in its training data, which stopped at a cutoff date. It knows nothing about my company's private documents, and if asked it may invent a fluent, wrong answer (a hallucination). RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, fixes this: at question time I search my documents, paste the few most relevant passages into the prompt, and ask the model to answer from them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three words, three steps. Retrieve: find the passages most relevant to the question. Augment: put them in the prompt. Generate: the model writes the answer using them.

question --> search your documents --> top passages
         --> prompt = instructions + passages + question
         --> LLM --> answer (with sources)

Why it works: the model is good at reading and summarising text that is in front of it (its context window, the maximum number of tokens it can read at once), even when it never saw that text in training. So you move knowledge out of the model's memory and into a searchable store you control.

What you gain: private and fresh knowledge (update a document, not the model), citations (you know which passage was used), per-user access control (filter at search time), and deletion (remove the chunk and it is gone).

What you do not get: a guarantee of truth. The model can still ignore or misread the passages, and if search misses the right passage the model cannot recover it. Retrieval quality caps answer quality.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not needed for this concept; see the prompt-building question (C0-Q075) for the full generate step.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying RAG "removes" hallucination. It reduces it.
  • Describing RAG as only "a vector database". The database is one stage of several.
  • Forgetting the access-control and citation benefits, which are often the real business reason.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does the "retrieval" actually search? → Usually embeddings of document chunks in a vector store, often combined with keyword (BM25) search.
  2. Where does RAG fail first? → In retrieval: wrong or missing chunks in the top results.
  3. Does RAG need a bigger model? → Often no; a mid-size model reading good passages beats a large model guessing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "give the model extra context from a vector DB." Senior: explains the knowledge-cutoff problem, lists the operational benefits (freshness, citations, ACLs, deletion) and says retrieval quality is the ceiling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A support bot answered with last year's refund policy until the team realised the model had never seen the new one; adding RAG over the help centre fixed it without any retraining.

questions.subtopic: RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context
questions.promptHtml: A colleague says "just put all our docs in the prompt" and another says "fine-tune the model on our docs". When would you choose RAG instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can pick the right tool and justify it with cost, freshness and control, not fashion.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Pasting everything works only for tiny corpora: the context window is limited, cost and latency grow with every token on every call, and quality drops when the prompt is full of noise. Fine-tuning (training the model further) is good for style and output format, but bad at injecting facts: it is slow to update, gives no citations, and cannot reliably delete data. RAG searches at question time, so it handles large, private, changing knowledge cheaply, with sources and per-user filtering.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Approach Good for Weak at
Paste everything Corpora of a few pages Cost per call, latency, token limits, "lost in the middle"
Fine-tuning Tone, format, narrow behaviour Fresh facts, citations, deleting data, retraining cost
RAG Large, private, changing knowledge Needs a good search step; extra moving parts

Arithmetic that makes it concrete. Say a corpus is 2 million tokens and you answer 10,000 questions a day. Pasting it is impossible for most models; even if a window were large enough, you would pay for millions of input tokens per call. With RAG you send about 3,000 tokens per call (5 chunks of 500 plus question and instructions), so cost and latency are small and flat.

They also combine: fine-tune for house style, use RAG for facts. "Long context makes RAG obsolete" is a trap: big windows still cost money per call, still degrade with noise, and give you no access control or source links.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not needed; this is a decision question.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "RAG replaces fine-tuning." They solve different problems (facts vs behaviour).
  • Thinking fine-tuning is the way to "teach the model our wiki".
  • Ignoring per-call cost when proposing the paste-everything design.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is paste-everything fine? → A few pages, low traffic, prototype stage.
  2. When is fine-tuning right? → Consistent tone or strict output format that prompting cannot achieve.
  3. Can you use both? → Yes: a tuned model for style, retrieval for facts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "RAG is cheaper than fine-tuning." Senior: frames facts vs behaviour, does the token-cost arithmetic, and mentions ACLs, citations and deletion.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team fine-tuned on their wiki, then spent two weeks failing to remove one customer's leaked document from the model; with RAG it would have been one delete call.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through a RAG pipeline end to end. Which parts run offline and which run on every question?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most basic whiteboard question. It reveals whether you understand the two phases and what must stay consistent between them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: There are two phases. Ingestion runs ahead of time: load documents, extract text, split into chunks, embed each chunk into a vector (a list of numbers capturing meaning), and store vector, text and metadata in a vector store. Query time runs on every question: embed the question with the same model, search for the top-K nearest chunks, optionally rerank, build the prompt, call the LLM, and return the answer with sources.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
INGESTION (offline / scheduled)
 documents --> parse --> chunk --> embed --> vector store (+ metadata)

QUERY (online, per request)
 question --> embed --> top-K search --> [rerank] --> prompt --> LLM --> answer + citations

Why split? Embedding a million chunks is slow and costs money, so it is done once. At query time you embed one short question and do a fast nearest-neighbour search, so retrieval takes tens of milliseconds and the LLM call dominates latency.

Invariants to protect:

  • Same embedding model for chunks and questions (otherwise vectors live in different spaces).
  • Chunk IDs and metadata that let you update, delete, filter and cite.
  • Logging of retrieved IDs and scores per request, so you can debug later.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: See the per-stage questions (chunking C0-Q072, store and search C0-Q073, generation C0-Q075).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a different embedding model at query time than at ingest.
  • Tuning only the LLM prompt while the real problem is chunking.
  • Not planning how documents get updated or deleted.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does most latency come from? → The LLM call; then reranker; vector search is usually small.
  2. What would you log? → Question, retrieved chunk IDs and scores, prompt tokens, latency per stage, answer, feedback.
  3. What if the source documents change hourly? → Incremental ingestion by content hash (see C0-Q084).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists the stages. Senior adds invariants (same model, stable IDs, metadata), where failures occur, and observability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reindex job accidentally embedded with a newer model while queries still used the old one; every answer became nonsense until the index was rebuilt.

questions.promptHtml: Why do we split documents into chunks before embedding, and how would you implement a basic splitter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Chunking quietly decides retrieval quality. A candidate who can explain and code it has actually built RAG.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A chunk is a small piece of a document, around one idea, which is the unit we search over. If I embedded a whole 50-page PDF, every topic would blur into one vector and I could not paste it all into the prompt anyway. A simple default is fixed-size windows (say 500 tokens) with some overlap (50 to 100) so a sentence cut at a boundary still appears whole in the neighbour, plus metadata like source and heading.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
An embedding has a fixed size (for example 1024 numbers) no matter how long the text is. Long text is squeezed into the same size, so the vector becomes an average of many topics and matches nothing precisely. Tiny chunks go the other way: "within 30 days" with no mention of refunds is useless.

Strategies:

  • Fixed size with overlap: simple, a fine first version.
  • Structure-aware: split on headings, paragraphs, Markdown sections, code functions.
  • Semantic: split where the topic changes; more expensive.
  • Parent-child: search small chunks, send the larger parent section to the model.

Always keep the heading path ("Billing > Refunds") with the chunk. A real system counts tokens; the code below uses words to stay simple.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def chunk(text: str, size: int = 200, overlap: int = 40) -> list[str]:
    words = text.split()
    step = size - overlap
    return [" ".join(words[i:i + size]) for i in range(0, max(len(words) - overlap, 1), step)]

print(len(chunk("word " * 1000)))  # prints 7
fun chunk(text: String, size: Int = 200, overlap: Int = 40): List<String> {
    val words = text.split(Regex("\\s+")).filter { it.isNotEmpty() }
    val step = size - overlap
    return (0 until maxOf(words.size - overlap, 1) step step)
        .map { words.subList(it, minOf(it + size, words.size)).joinToString(" ") }
}

fun main() = println(chunk("word ".repeat(1000)).size) // prints 7
import java.util.*;

public class Chunker {
    static List<String> chunk(String text, int size, int overlap) {
        String[] w = text.trim().split("\\s+");
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        int step = size - overlap;
        for (int i = 0; i < Math.max(w.length - overlap, 1); i += step) {
            out.add(String.join(" ", Arrays.copyOfRange(w, i, Math.min(i + size, w.length))));
        }
        return out;
    }

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(chunk("word ".repeat(1000), 200, 40).size()); // prints 7
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Picking a chunk size by gut feeling instead of measuring retrieval.
  • Splitting mid-table or mid-code-block.
  • Dropping metadata, which blocks filters, citations and access control.
  • Leaving headers, footers and menus in the text, which pollutes search.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why overlap? → So a fact straddling a boundary is complete in at least one chunk.
  2. Tokens or characters? → Tokens match the model's limits; characters are a rough proxy.
  3. What is parent-child retrieval? → Match on small chunks for precision, return the bigger parent for context.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "split into 500 tokens." Senior: explains the averaging effect, uses structure-aware splitting, stores heading paths and IDs, and tunes size with recall.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A pricing table was split in half across two chunks; the model quoted the price of the wrong plan until tables were kept whole as Markdown.

questions.promptHtml: How do you embed and store chunks, and how does a similarity search over them work? Write a minimal version.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Verifies you understand vectors, cosine similarity and what a vector store actually does, beyond calling a library.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An embedding model turns each chunk into a vector, a list of numbers where texts with similar meaning point in similar directions. I store the vector, the chunk text and metadata. To search, I embed the question with the same model and rank chunks by cosine similarity (1 means same direction, 0 unrelated). If vectors are normalised to length 1, cosine equals a plain dot product, which is cheap. At scale I use an ANN (approximate nearest neighbour) index such as HNSW.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each store row: id, vector, text, metadata. FAISS is an in-process library, pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension (SQL filters and transactions), Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus and Pinecone are dedicated vector databases. The vector dimension is fixed by the model, and the store must be created with that exact dimension.

Exact search compares the query against every vector: fine for tens of thousands of chunks, too slow for millions, where ANN indexes trade a little recall for big speed.

Anthropic does not offer its own embedding model; its docs point to providers such as Voyage AI (verify in the docs). Others: OpenAI text-embedding-3-*, Cohere, Gemini, or local models such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2. The embed function below is a stand-in you replace with a real call.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import numpy as np

def embed(texts: list[str]) -> np.ndarray:
    # Replace with a real provider call; return shape (n, dim), rows L2-normalised.
    raise NotImplementedError

class Store:
    def __init__(self):
        self.vecs, self.items = [], []

    def add(self, chunks: list[str], source: str):
        v = embed(chunks)
        self.vecs.extend(v)
        self.items.extend({"text": c, "source": source} for c in chunks)

    def search(self, qvec, k=4):
        scores = np.array(self.vecs) @ qvec          # cosine, since normalised
        top = np.argsort(-scores)[:k]
        return [(float(scores[i]), self.items[i]) for i in top]
data class Item(val text: String, val source: String)

fun embed(texts: List<String>): List<FloatArray> = TODO("call embedding provider; L2-normalise")

fun dot(a: FloatArray, b: FloatArray) = a.indices.sumOf { (a[it] * b[it]).toDouble() }

class Store {
    private val vecs = mutableListOf<FloatArray>()
    private val items = mutableListOf<Item>()

    fun add(chunks: List<String>, source: String) {
        vecs += embed(chunks)
        items += chunks.map { Item(it, source) }
    }

    fun search(q: FloatArray, k: Int = 4): List<Pair<Double, Item>> =
        vecs.indices.map { dot(vecs[it], q) to items[it] }
            .sortedByDescending { it.first }.take(k)
}
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class Store {
    record Item(String text, String source) {}
    record Hit(double score, Item item) {}

    final List<float[]> vecs = new ArrayList<>();
    final List<Item> items = new ArrayList<>();

    // Stand-in: call your embedding provider and L2-normalise.
    static List<float[]> embed(List<String> texts) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }

    static double dot(float[] a, float[] b) {
        double s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) s += a[i] * b[i]; return s;
    }

    void add(List<String> chunks, String source) {
        vecs.addAll(embed(chunks));
        chunks.forEach(c -> items.add(new Item(c, source)));
    }

    List<Hit> search(float[] q, int k) {
        return IntStream.range(0, vecs.size())
            .mapToObj(i -> new Hit(dot(vecs.get(i), q), items.get(i)))
            .sorted(Comparator.comparingDouble(Hit::score).reversed())
            .limit(k).collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Different embedding models or dimensions at ingest and query time.
  • Assuming dot product equals cosine without normalising.
  • Some APIs distinguish "document" and "query" input types; forgetting this lowers quality (verify per provider).
  • Not recording the model name with each vector, which makes later migration painful.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not store text in the vector DB only? → You need text for the prompt and metadata for filters and citations.
  2. What is HNSW? → A graph index that finds near neighbours quickly, approximately.
  3. Why batch embedding calls? → Fewer round trips and better rate-limit use; retry with backoff.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "put embeddings in Pinecone." Senior: explains cosine vs dot with normalisation, fixed dimension, upserts keyed by chunk ID, model versioning and ANN recall trade-offs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An ingest job crashed on a dimension error after a model change, because the table was still created for the old vector size.

questions.promptHtml: What are top-K and metadata filters in retrieval, and how do you pick K?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: K is the first knob everyone turns. Filters are where security bugs live.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Top-K is how many of the best-scoring chunks the search returns. Metadata filters restrict the search to chunks with certain attributes, such as tenant_id = 42, language, date or the user's permission groups. Without a reranker I use a small K (3 to 8) since all of it goes to the model; with a reranker I retrieve more (20 to 50) and rerank down. Filters must be applied inside the search query, never in the UI afterwards.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Too small a K misses the right chunk (low recall). Too large a K adds cost (tokens), latency and noise that makes the model drift. The right K is found by measuring Recall@K on a golden set (see C0-Q081), not by feel.

Filters are applied before or during the vector search by the store (pgvector uses a SQL WHERE, Qdrant has payload filters). Never retrieve everything and hide results client-side: chunks the user may not see would already be in the prompt, so the model can quote them.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not needed here; the filter is a store parameter. Example pgvector SQL: SELECT text FROM chunks WHERE tenant_id = $1 ORDER BY embedding <=> $2 LIMIT 5; (<=> is cosine distance in pgvector; verify operator for your index).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Filtering after retrieval, so the top-K is filled with chunks that are then discarded.
  • Forgetting the tenant filter altogether.
  • A large K "to be safe", which hurts both cost and quality.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if a filter leaves fewer than K results? → Return fewer; do not pad with unrelated chunks.
  2. Pre-filter vs post-filter? → Pre/in-search filtering keeps K results; post-filtering can return nothing.
  3. How do you test the filter? → An automated test where tenant A asks about tenant B's document and must get no hits.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "K = 5." Senior: ties K to a reranker design and measured recall, and treats filters as a security boundary with tests.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A bot returned another customer's contract text because the tenant check lived in the front end instead of the query.

questions.promptHtml: Show how you would build the prompt from retrieved chunks and call the model so that it answers only from them.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The generate step is where grounding is won or lost. They want to see delimiters, numbered sources, a "don't know" rule and sensible parameters.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The system prompt (standing instructions) says: answer only from the provided documents, cite them by ID, and say "I don't know" if the answer is missing. The user message contains the chunks, each wrapped in a tag with an ID and source, then the question. I use a low temperature (0 to 0.2) for factual answers and set max_tokens high enough that the answer is not cut off. The API key comes from an environment variable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
[system]  Answer ONLY from <documents>. Cite as [id]. If not found, say "I don't know".
[user]    <documents>
            <doc id="1" source="refund-policy.md">Refunds within 30 days...</doc>
            <doc id="2" source="faq.md">Digital goods are non-refundable...</doc>
          </documents>
          Question: Can I get a refund after 45 days?

Tags separate your instructions from document text, which may itself contain hostile instructions (prompt injection, see C0-Q090). The token budget is system + question + K chunks + answer, and it must fit the context window; cost and time-to-first-token grow with it. Some newer models restrict sampling parameters such as temperature; check the docs for your model.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

SYSTEM = ("Answer ONLY from the documents. Cite sources like [1]. "
          "If the documents do not contain the answer, reply exactly: I don't know.")

def answer(question: str, hits: list[dict]) -> str:
    docs = "\n".join(f'<doc id="{i+1}" source="{h["source"]}">{h["text"]}</doc>'
                     for i, h in enumerate(hits))
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=500, temperature=0, system=SYSTEM,
        messages=[{"role": "user",
                   "content": f"<documents>\n{docs}\n</documents>\n\nQuestion: {question}"}])
    return msg.content[0].text   # e.g. "No, refunds end after 30 days [1]."

import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams

    val docs = hits.mapIndexed { i, (src, text) -> """<doc id="${i + 1}" source="$src">$text</doc>""" }
        .joinToString("\n")
    val params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
        .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(500).temperature(0.0).system(SYSTEM)
        .addUserMessage("<documents>\n$docs\n</documents>\n\nQuestion: $question")
